intro: Hi! At B1 you used who, which, that and where to say which person or thing you mean: the office where I work. Today you add extra information with commas, use whose, whom and which for a whole idea, and make clauses shorter: the man standing there. Warm-up: what's the difference between 'My sister who lives in Medan' and 'My sister, who lives in Medan'?
teachingNotes: Recap in one line (B1): a defining relative clause says WHICH person or thing we mean (the man who lives next door), no commas, that is fine, and an object pronoun can be left out (the book I bought). New here: a NON-defining clause adds extra information about someone or something already identified (a name, my father, our office, Bandung) and sits between commas, like brackets; at the end of a sentence it needs one comma (I had lunch with Rina, who works at a startup). Key example: My father, who lives in Bandung, is a doctor. Without commas it sounds as if you have several fathers and mean the one in Bandung. In speech the commas are short pauses.

Both 'My sister who lives in Medan is a nurse' (I have several sisters; the one in Medan) and 'My sister, who lives in Medan, is a nurse' (I have one sister; Medan is a bonus fact) are correct, with different meanings. Only test commas with a context that decides it (only one brother, a name, two laptops). Typed answers are normalised (punctuation removed), so test commas with A/B or multiple choice, never with typed sentences. Indonesian writers often drop these commas because 'yang' works either way; in English they change the meaning.

Common errors: (1) missing commas: *My father who lives in Bandung is a doctor → My father, who lives in Bandung, is a doctor. (2) that in a non-defining clause: *The company, that I work for, is growing → which. (3) leaving the pronoun out in a non-defining clause: *Pak Hasan, I met in Bali, … → Pak Hasan, who (whom) I met in Bali, … (allowed in defining clauses only). where works in non-defining clauses too (Surabaya, where my parents live, …). British vs American: American style guides prefer that for defining clauses and which only with commas; British English uses which in both. With commas, both use which.

whose = possession, Indonesian 'yang …-nya' (pria yang mobilnya dicuri → the man whose car was stolen); for people and also companies/things (a startup whose app…). Traps: *the man who his car was stolen; who's (= who is/has) sounds the same. whom = object form of who, formal (emails, reports), and required after a preposition: to whom, with whom, for whom (never *to who). In everyday speech who is fine as an object, or leave it out and put the preposition at the end (the client I sent the invoice to): say so. Never whom as subject (*the woman whom lives next door). Don't test who vs whom as competing correct options except after a preposition.

which for a whole clause: He didn't call, which was strange (what was strange = the fact that he didn't call). Always a comma before it. Indonesian '…, dan itu aneh / hal itu membuat…' leads to *', what was strange', *', that was strange' or *', it was strange' (two sentences joined by a comma). Only which is correct.

Reduced relatives: only when who/which/that is the subject and is followed by be: who is standing → standing (the man standing there), which was written → written (the report written by Rina). The V3 (past participle) is taught here only as the reduction of a passive clause the learner knows from B1 (present/past simple passive). Common error 3: *The man is standing there is my boss (only who dropped); also *the report which written by Rina (only was dropped). -ing can also replace a present simple state (people living in Jakarta = who live), but not one finished action (the man who called yesterday, not *the man calling yesterday). Not in this lesson: adverbial participle clauses (Having finished…, Walking home, I…), reduced non-defining clauses, when as a relative word, third conditional, past modals.

keyPoints.title: Extra information goes between commas
keyPoints.explanation: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information about someone or something we already know (a name, my father, our office). Put it between commas: My father, who lives in Bandung, is a doctor. Without commas it would mean you have several fathers. With commas use who (people), which (things) or where (places), never that, and never leave the word out.

id.title: Informasi tambahan diletakkan di antara koma
id.explanation: Non-defining relative clause menambahkan informasi tambahan tentang orang atau benda yang sudah jelas (sebuah nama, ayah saya, kantor kami). Letakkan di antara koma: My father, who lives in Bandung, is a doctor. Tanpa koma, artinya seolah-olah ayahmu lebih dari satu. Dengan koma pakai who (orang), which (benda) atau where (tempat), tidak pernah that, dan kata itu tidak boleh dihilangkan.

keyPoints.title: whose, whom, and which for a whole idea
keyPoints.explanation: whose shows belonging, like 'yang …-nya': the man whose car was stolen (not 'who his car'). whom is a formal who for the person who receives the action, used after to, with, for: the client to whom I sent the invoice. In speech, who or no word is fine: the client I sent the invoice to. After a comma, which can mean the whole idea before it: He didn't call, which was strange.

examples.en: He didn't call, which was strange.
examples.id: Dia tidak menelepon, dan itu aneh.

id.title: whose, whom, dan which untuk seluruh ide
id.explanation: whose menunjukkan kepemilikan, seperti 'yang …-nya': the man whose car was stolen (bukan 'who his car'). whom adalah bentuk formal who untuk orang yang dikenai tindakan, dipakai setelah to, with, for: the client to whom I sent the invoice. Saat bicara, who atau tanpa kata pun tidak apa-apa: the client I sent the invoice to. Setelah koma, which bisa berarti seluruh ide sebelumnya: He didn't call, which was strange.

keyPoints.title: Shorter clauses: drop who/which + be
keyPoints.explanation: When who/which is followed by is, are, was or were, you can drop both words. Keep the -ing form for something happening (the man who is standing there → the man standing there) or the third form (V3) for a passive meaning (the report which was written by Rina → the report written by Rina). Drop both words, not only one: 'The man is standing there is my boss' is wrong.

examples.en: The man standing there is my boss.
examples.id: Pria yang berdiri di sana adalah atasan saya. (= who is standing)

examples.en: The report written by Rina was excellent.
examples.id: Laporan yang ditulis oleh Rina bagus sekali. (= which was written)

id.title: Klausa ringkas: buang who/which + be
id.explanation: Kalau setelah who/which ada is, are, was atau were, kamu bisa membuang kedua kata itu. Pakai bentuk -ing untuk sesuatu yang sedang terjadi (the man who is standing there → the man standing there) atau bentuk ketiga (V3) untuk arti pasif (the report which was written by Rina → the report written by Rina). Buang dua-duanya, jangan cuma satu: 'The man is standing there is my boss' salah.

assessment.prompt:
Rina has only one brother. Which sentence is correct? Write A or B.
A: My brother who works at a bank in Surabaya is getting married.
B: My brother, who works at a bank in Surabaya, is getting married.
assessment.rubric: Correct: B. Rina has only one brother, so 'who works at a bank in Surabaya' is extra information and goes between commas. A (no commas) suggests she has several brothers and means the one in Surabaya = 0.

assessment.prompt:
One word in this sentence is wrong. Write the correct word.
Our company, that opened its first office in Surabaya in 2015, now has 300 employees.
acceptableAnswers: our company which opened its first office in surabaya in 2015 now has 300 employees
assessment.rubric: Correct: which (a clause between commas never starts with that; a company is a thing). 'who' = 20 (who is for people). Leaving the word out = 0 (it can't be left out with commas). Writing 'that' again = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete with one word: We need to call the customer ___ order arrived damaged.
assessment.rubric: Correct: whose (the order belongs to the customer: pelanggan yang pesanannya rusak). 'who's' = 20 (sounds the same but means who is). 'who', 'which' or 'that' = 0 (they can't show belonging).

assessment.prompt: This is from a formal email. Complete with one word: The manager to ___ you sent your application is on leave until Monday.
assessment.rubric: Correct: whom (after a preposition like 'to', formal English needs whom). 'who' = 40 (heard in casual speech, but not after 'to' in a formal email). 'which' or 'that' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete with one word: Budi didn't reply to any of my messages, ___ I found really strange.
assessment.rubric: Correct: which (it refers to the whole idea: the fact that Budi didn't reply). 'that' = 20 (that can't follow a comma here). 'what' or 'it' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Make the sentence shorter by taking out two words: The woman who is sitting next to Pak Hasan is our new finance director.
acceptableAnswers: the woman sitting next to pak hasan is our new finance director
assessment.rubric: Correct: The woman sitting next to Pak Hasan is our new finance director (drop 'who is'). Dropping only 'who' (The woman is sitting next to Pak Hasan is…) = 20. Dropping only 'is' (The woman who sitting…) = 20. The original sentence unchanged = 0.

assessment.prompt: Make the sentence shorter by taking out two words: All the photos which were taken at the wedding are on Google Drive.
acceptableAnswers: all the photos taken at the wedding are on google drive
assessment.rubric: Correct: All the photos taken at the wedding are on Google Drive (drop 'which were', keep the V3 'taken'). 'which taken' = 20 (only were dropped). 'were taken' without which (All the photos were taken at the wedding are…) = 20. Changing taken to 'taking' = 30 (the photos didn't take anything).

blocks.text:
At B1 you learnt **defining** relative clauses: they tell us **which** person or thing you mean (*the man **who lives next door***). Without them, we don't know who you're talking about.
A **non-defining** relative clause is different. We already know exactly who or what it is, and the clause just adds **extra information**, like a note in brackets. It goes between **commas**: *My father, **who lives in Bandung**, is a doctor.* You have only one father, so *who lives in Bandung* doesn't tell us which father; it's a bonus fact. Take it out and the sentence still works: *My father is a doctor.*
**Why the commas matter:** *My father who lives in Bandung is a doctor* (no commas) sounds as if you have **several fathers** and you mean the one in Bandung. Strange!
If the clause ends the sentence, you need only one comma: *I had lunch with Rina, **who works at a startup in Jakarta**.*

id.text:
Di B1 kamu sudah belajar **defining** relative clause: bagian ini menjelaskan orang atau benda **yang mana** yang kamu maksud (*the man **who lives next door***). Tanpa bagian itu, kita tidak tahu siapa yang kamu bicarakan.
**Non-defining** relative clause berbeda. Kita sudah tahu persis siapa atau apa yang dimaksud, dan klausa itu hanya menambahkan **informasi tambahan**, seperti catatan dalam kurung. Letaknya di antara **koma**: *My father, **who lives in Bandung**, is a doctor.* Ayahmu cuma satu, jadi *who lives in Bandung* tidak menjelaskan ayah yang mana; itu hanya info bonus. Kalau dihapus, kalimatnya tetap utuh: *My father is a doctor.*
**Kenapa koma itu penting:** *My father who lives in Bandung is a doctor* (tanpa koma) terdengar seolah-olah ayahmu **lebih dari satu** dan yang kamu maksud adalah yang di Bandung. Aneh, kan!
Kalau klausanya ada di akhir kalimat, cukup satu koma: *I had lunch with Rina, **who works at a startup in Jakarta**.*

material.title: With commas: no that, and never leave it out

blocks.text:
Two rules for clauses between commas:
- Use **who** for people, **which** for things and **where** for places, but **never that**: *The company, **which** I work for, is growing* (not *'The company, that I work for'*). At B1 *that* was fine; with commas it isn't.
- **Never leave the word out**, even when a person comes next. Without commas you can say *the book I bought*, but with commas it must stay: *Dimas, **who** I worked with in Surabaya, …* (not *'Dimas, I worked with in Surabaya, …'*).

id.text:
Dua aturan untuk klausa di antara koma:
- Pakai **who** untuk orang, **which** untuk benda dan **where** untuk tempat, tapi **tidak pernah that**: *The company, **which** I work for, is growing* (bukan *'The company, that I work for'*). Di B1 *that* boleh; dengan koma tidak boleh.
- **Kata itu tidak boleh dihilangkan**, walaupun setelahnya ada orang. Tanpa koma kamu boleh bilang *the book I bought*, tapi dengan koma kata itu wajib ada: *Dimas, **who** I worked with in Surabaya, …* (bukan *'Dimas, I worked with in Surabaya, …'*).

blocks.text: **British vs American:** without commas, many American style guides prefer **that** (*the app that I use*), while British English happily uses **which** too. With commas, both agree: **which**, never that.

id.text: **Inggris Britania vs Amerika:** tanpa koma, banyak panduan gaya Amerika lebih suka **that** (*the app that I use*), sedangkan bahasa Inggris Britania juga biasa memakai **which**. Dengan koma, keduanya sepakat: **which**, tidak pernah that.

id.title: Dengan koma: tanpa that, dan jangan dihilangkan

blocks.text:
**whose** shows that something **belongs** to someone. It's Indonesian **yang …-nya**: *pria yang mobil**nya** dicuri* → *the man **whose** car was stolen*. Don't translate word by word: *'the man who his car was stolen'* ✗. **whose** works for people and also for companies and things: *a startup **whose** app is used by millions*.
**who's** sounds the same (like 'huuz') but means **who is** or **who has**: *Who's that?* It's a different word.
**whom** is the **object** form of who: the person who **receives** the action, not the one who does it. It's **formal** (emails, reports, speeches) and is used especially after a **preposition** (a little word like *to, with, for*): *the client **to whom** I sent the invoice*, *the people **with whom** I work*. After a preposition it must be **whom**, never *'to who'*.
**In everyday speech** people just say **who**, or leave the word out and put the preposition at the end: *the client (who) I sent the invoice to*. That's completely natural.

id.text:
**whose** menunjukkan bahwa sesuatu **milik** seseorang. Artinya seperti **yang …-nya**: *pria yang mobil**nya** dicuri* → *the man **whose** car was stolen*. Jangan diterjemahkan kata per kata: *'the man who his car was stolen'* ✗. **whose** bisa untuk orang, juga untuk perusahaan dan benda: *a startup **whose** app is used by millions*.
**who's** bunyinya sama (seperti 'huuz') tapi artinya **who is** atau **who has**: *Who's that?* Itu kata yang berbeda.
**whom** adalah bentuk **objek** dari who: orang yang **dikenai** tindakan, bukan yang melakukannya. Kata ini **formal** (email, laporan, pidato) dan dipakai terutama setelah **preposisi** (kata kecil seperti *to, with, for*): *the client **to whom** I sent the invoice*, *the people **with whom** I work*. Setelah preposisi harus **whom**, bukan *'to who'*.
**Saat bicara sehari-hari** orang cukup bilang **who**, atau menghilangkan katanya dan menaruh preposisi di akhir: *the client (who) I sent the invoice to*. Itu sangat wajar.

blocks.text: Don't use **whom** for the person who does the action: *'the woman whom lives next door'* ✗ → *the woman **who** lives next door*. If you're not sure, **who** is always safe in conversation; just remember **to whom / with whom / for whom** for formal writing.

id.text: Jangan pakai **whom** untuk orang yang melakukan tindakan: *'the woman whom lives next door'* ✗ → *the woman **who** lives next door*. Kalau ragu, **who** selalu aman dalam percakapan; cukup ingat **to whom / with whom / for whom** untuk tulisan formal.

blocks.prompt: Sari is the colleague ___ presentation won the award.
blocks.explain: The presentation belongs to Sari (rekan yang presentasinya menang), so use whose. who's means 'who is', and who can't show belonging.

blocks.text:
Usually **which** points to one thing just before it. But after a comma, **which** can point to the **whole idea** before it: *He didn't call, **which** was strange.* What was strange? Not 'him', but **the fact that he didn't call**.
In Indonesian you'd say *…, dan itu aneh* or *…, hal itu membuat saya kaget*. Don't translate it as:
- *'He didn't call, **what** was strange'* ✗ (what isn't used like this)
- *'He didn't call, **that** was strange'* ✗ (no that after a comma)
- *'He didn't call, **it** was strange'* ✗ (two sentences joined only by a comma: use a full stop, or **which**)
There is always a **comma** before this which.

id.text:
Biasanya **which** menunjuk satu benda tepat sebelumnya. Tapi setelah koma, **which** bisa menunjuk **seluruh ide** sebelumnya: *He didn't call, **which** was strange.* Apa yang aneh? Bukan 'dia', tapi **kenyataan bahwa dia tidak menelepon**.
Dalam bahasa Indonesia kamu akan bilang *…, dan itu aneh* atau *…, hal itu membuat saya kaget*. Jangan diterjemahkan jadi:
- *'He didn't call, **what** was strange'* ✗ (what tidak dipakai seperti ini)
- *'He didn't call, **that** was strange'* ✗ (tidak ada that setelah koma)
- *'He didn't call, **it** was strange'* ✗ (dua kalimat disambung hanya dengan koma: pakai titik, atau **which**)
Selalu ada **koma** sebelum which yang seperti ini.

id.note: which = kenyataan bahwa dia tidak menelepon

blocks.text:
When **who/which/that** is followed by **is, are, was** or **were**, you can often drop **both words** and keep the rest. This is a **reduced relative clause** (a shortened 'yang' clause).
- With **-ing**, when the person or thing is doing something: *the man **who is standing** there* → *the man **standing** there*.
- With the **third form** (**V3**, the form you know from passive sentences: *written, made, taken*): *the report **which was written** by Rina* → *the report **written** by Rina*. The meaning is still passive: the report didn't write anything; Rina wrote it.
**Drop both words, not just one:** *'The man is standing there is my boss'* ✗ (two verbs, is … is, for one subject), *'the report which written by Rina'* ✗.
Indonesian is short here too: *laporan yang ditulis oleh Rina* = *the report written by Rina*.

id.text:
Kalau setelah **who/which/that** ada **is, are, was** atau **were**, kamu sering bisa membuang **kedua kata itu** dan mempertahankan sisanya. Ini disebut **reduced relative clause** (klausa 'yang' yang diringkas).
- Dengan **-ing**, kalau orang atau benda itu sedang melakukan sesuatu: *the man **who is standing** there* → *the man **standing** there*.
- Dengan **bentuk ketiga** (**V3**, bentuk yang kamu kenal dari kalimat pasif: *written, made, taken*): *the report **which was written** by Rina* → *the report **written** by Rina*. Artinya tetap pasif: laporannya tidak menulis apa-apa; Rina yang menulisnya.
**Buang dua-duanya, jangan cuma satu:** *'The man is standing there is my boss'* ✗ (dua kata kerja, is … is, untuk satu subjek), *'the report which written by Rina'* ✗.
Bahasa Indonesia juga ringkas di sini: *laporan yang ditulis oleh Rina* = *the report written by Rina*.

blocks.text: You can only shorten it like this when **who/which is the one doing it** (followed by *is/are/was/were*). *the man who I met* can only lose **who** (*the man I met*, as at B1), never become *'the man meeting'*. You'll also see **-ing** for things that are generally true: *people **living** in Jakarta* (= who live in Jakarta). But for one finished action, keep the full clause: *the man **who called** yesterday*, not *'the man calling yesterday'*.

id.text: Kamu hanya bisa meringkas seperti ini kalau **who/which adalah pelakunya** (diikuti *is/are/was/were*). *the man who I met* hanya bisa kehilangan **who** (*the man I met*, seperti di B1), tidak pernah jadi *'the man meeting'*. Kamu juga akan melihat **-ing** untuk hal yang umumnya benar: *people **living** in Jakarta* (= who live in Jakarta). Tapi untuk satu tindakan yang sudah selesai, pakai klausa lengkap: *the man **who called** yesterday*, bukan *'the man calling yesterday'*.

blocks.prompt: Which is the correct short version of: The people who are waiting outside want to see you.
options: The people are waiting outside want to see you.
The people waiting outside want to see you.
The people who waiting outside want to see you.
blocks.explain: Drop both who and are, and keep waiting. The other two drop only one word, which leaves a broken sentence.

id.prompt: Mana versi ringkas yang benar dari: The people who are waiting outside want to see you.
id.explain: Buang who dan are sekaligus, lalu pertahankan waiting. Dua pilihan lainnya hanya membuang satu kata, jadi kalimatnya rusak.

id.intro: Hai! Di B1 kamu sudah memakai who, which, that dan where untuk menjelaskan orang atau benda yang mana yang kamu maksud: the office where I work. Hari ini kamu belajar menambahkan informasi tambahan dengan koma, memakai whose, whom dan which untuk seluruh ide, serta meringkas klausa: the man standing there. Pemanasan: apa bedanya 'My sister who lives in Medan' dan 'My sister, who lives in Medan'?

assessment.rca-1:
Rina hanya punya satu saudara laki-laki. Kalimat mana yang benar? Tulis A atau B.
A: My brother who works at a bank in Surabaya is getting married.
B: My brother, who works at a bank in Surabaya, is getting married.
assessment.rca-2:
Ada satu kata yang salah dalam kalimat ini. Tulis kata yang benar.
Our company, that opened its first office in Surabaya in 2015, now has 300 employees.
assessment.rca-3: Lengkapi dengan satu kata: We need to call the customer ___ order arrived damaged.
assessment.rca-4: Ini dari email formal. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: The manager to ___ you sent your application is on leave until Monday.
assessment.rca-5: Lengkapi dengan satu kata: Budi didn't reply to any of my messages, ___ I found really strange.
assessment.rca-6: Buat kalimat ini lebih ringkas dengan menghapus dua kata: The woman who is sitting next to Pak Hasan is our new finance director.
assessment.rca-7: Buat kalimat ini lebih ringkas dengan menghapus dua kata: All the photos which were taken at the wedding are on Google Drive.
